reference.answer: Section 38A of the General Insurance Business (Nationalisation) Act, 1972, titled "Powers of Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India not to apply to International Financial Services Centre," is the provision in question[1]. It provides that, notwithstanding anything in any other law, the powers exercisable by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India under the Act do not extend to an International Financial Services Centre set up under sub-section (1) of section 18 of the Special Economic Zones Act, 2005, and that such powers, insofar as they concern regulation of financial products, financial services and financial institutions permitted in such Centres, are instead exercisable by the International Financial Services Centres Authority established under sub-section (1) of section 4 of the International Financial Services Centres Authority Act, 2019[1].

reference.answer: Article 239B of the Constitution of India empowers the administrator of the Union territory of Puducherry, when its Legislature is not in session and he is satisfied that immediate action is necessary, to promulgate an Ordinance, provided he first obtains the President's instructions[1]. Such an Ordinance, promulgated in pursuance of the President's instructions, is deemed to be an Act of the Legislature of the Union territory duly enacted[1].

reference.answer: Under Section 120A, "criminal conspiracy" means an agreement between two or more persons to do, or cause to be done, either (1) an illegal act, or (2) an act which is not itself illegal but is to be carried out by illegal means[1]. A proviso limits this: if the agreement is not itself to commit an offence, mere agreement is not enough — some act besides the agreement must actually be done by one or more of the parties in pursuance of it before it amounts to a criminal conspiracy; an agreement to commit an offence, however, constitutes conspiracy without any further act[1]. The Explanation clarifies that it does not matter whether the illegal act is the ultimate object of the agreement or is merely incidental to that object[1].

The Court shall presume the genuineness of every electronic or digital record purporting to be the Official Gazette, or purporting to be electronic or digital record directed by any law to be kept by any person, if such electronic or digital record is kept substantially in the form required by law and is produced from proper custody. Explanation.--For the purposes of this section and section 93 electronic records are said to be in proper custody if they are in the place in which, and looked after by the person with whom such document is required to be kept; but no custody is improper if it is proved to have had a legitimate origin, or the circumstances of the particular case are such as to render that origin probable.

Primary evidence means the document itself produced for the inspection of the Court. Explanation 1.--Where a document is executed in several parts, each part is primary evidence of the document. Explanation 2.--Where a document is executed in counterpart, each counterpart being executed by one or some of the parties only, each counterpart is primary evidence as against the parties executing it Explanation 3.--Where a number of documents are all made by one uniform process, as in the case of printing, lithography or photography, each is primary evidence of the contents of the rest; but, where they are all copies of a common original, they are not primary evidence of the contents of the original. Explanation 4.--Where an electronic or digital record is created or stored, and such storage occurs simultaneously or sequentially in multiple files, each such file is primary evidence. Explanation 5.--Where an electronic or digital record is produced from proper custody, such electronic and digital record is primary evidence unless it is disputed. Explanation 6.--Where a video recording is simultaneously stored in electronic form and transmitted or broadcast or transferred to another, each of the stored recordings is primary evidence. Explanation 7.--Where an electronic or digital record is stored in multiple storage spaces in a computer resource, each such automated storage, including temporary files, is primary evidence. Illustration. A person is shown to have been in possession of a number of placards, all printed at one time from one original. Any one of the placards is primary evidence of the contents of any other, but no one of them is primary evidence of the contents of the original.

retrieved_context.text: Evidence may be given in any suit or proceeding of the existence or non-existence of every fact in issue and of such other facts as are hereinafter declared to be relevant, and of no others. Explanation.--This section shall not enable any person to give evidence of a fact which he is disentitled to prove by any provision of the law for the time being in force relating to civil procedure. Illustrations. (a) A is tried for the murder of B by beating him with a club with the intention of causing his death. At A's trial the following facts are in issue:-- A's beating B with the club; A's causing B's death by such beating; A's intention to cause B's death. (b) A suitor does not bring with him, and have in readiness for production at the first hearing of the case, a bond on which he relies. This section does not enable him to produce the bond or prove its contents at a subsequent stage of the proceedings, otherwise than in accordance with the conditions prescribed by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (5 of 1908).

retrieved_context.title: The Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 — Section 19 (Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf)
retrieved_context.section_heading: Proof of admissions against persons making them, and by or on their behalf
retrieved_context.text: Admissions are relevant and may be proved as against the person who makes them, or his representative in interest; but they cannot be proved by or on behalf of the person who makes them or by his representative in interest, except in the following cases, namely:-- (1) an admission may be proved by or on behalf of the person making it, when it is of such a nature that, if the person making it were dead, it would be relevant as between third persons under section 26; (2) an admission may be proved by or on behalf of the person making it, when it consists of a statement of the existence of any state of mind or body, relevant or in issue, made at or about the time when such state of mind or body existed, and is accompanied by conduct rendering its falsehood improbable; (3) an admission may be proved by or on behalf of the person making it, if it is relevant otherwise than as an admission. Illustrations. (a) The question between A and B is, whether a certain deed is or is not forged. A affirms that it is genuine, B that it is forged. A may prove a statement by B that the deed is genuine, and B may prove a statement by A that deed is forged; but A cannot prove a statement by himself that the deed is genuine, nor can B prove a statement by himself that the deed is forged. (b) A, the captain of a ship, is tried for casting her away. Evidence is given to show that the ship was taken out of her proper course. A produces a book kept by him in the ordinary course of his business showing observations alleged to have been taken by him from day to day, and indicating that the ship was not taken out of her proper course. A may prove these statements, because they would be admissible between third parties, if he were dead, under clause (b) of section 26. (c) A is accused of a crime committed by him at Kolkata. He produces a letter written by himself and dated at Chennai on that day, and bearing the Chennai post-mark of that day. The statement in the date of the letter is admissible, because, if A were dead, it would be admissible under clause (b) of section 26. (d) A is accused of receiving stolen goods knowing them to be stolen. He offers to prove that he refused to sell them below their value. A may prove these statements, though they are admissions, because they are explanatory of conduct influenced by facts in issue. (e) A is accused of fraudulently having in his possession counterfeit currency which he knew to be counterfeit. He offers to prove that he asked a skilful person to examine the currency as he doubted whether it was counterfeit or not, and that person did examine it and told him it was genuine. A may prove these facts.

reference.answer: Under Section 210 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, a person legally bound to produce or deliver up a document or electronic record to a public servant who intentionally omits to do so is punishable with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both[1]. retrieved_context.text: (1) In every inquiry or trial the proceedings shall be continued from day-to-day basis until all the witnesses in attendance have been examined, unless the Court finds the adjournment of the same beyond the following day to be necessary for reasons to be recorded: Provided that when the inquiry or trial relates to an offence under section 64, section 65, section 66, section 67, section 68, section 70 or section 71 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (45 of 2023) the inquiry or trial shall be completed within a period of two months from the date of filing of the chargesheet. (2) If the Court, after taking cognizance of an offence, or commencement of trial, finds it necessary or advisable to postpone the commencement of, or adjourn, any inquiry or trial, it may, from time to time, for reasons to be recorded, postpone or adjourn the same on such terms as it thinks fit, for such time as it considers reasonable, and may by a warrant remand the accused if in custody: Provided that no Court shall remand an accused person to custody under this section for a term exceeding fifteen days at a time: Provided further that when witnesses are in attendance, no adjournment or postponement shall be granted, without examining them, except for special reasons to be recorded in writing: Provided also that no adjournment shall be granted for the purpose only of enabling the accused person to show cause against the sentence proposed to be imposed on him: Provided also that--- (a) no adjournment shall be granted at the request of a party, except where the circumstances are beyond the control of that party; (b) where the circumstances are beyond the control of a party, not more than two adjournments may be granted by the Court after hearing the objections of the other party and for the reasons to be recorded in writing; (c) the fact that the advocate of a party is engaged in another Court, shall not be a ground for adjournment; (d) where a witness is present in Court but a party or his advocate is not present or the party or his advocate though present in Court, is not ready to examine or cross-examine the witness, the Court may, if thinks fit, record the statement of the witness and pass such orders as it thinks fit dispensing with the examination-in-chief or cross-examination of the witness, as the case may be. reference.answer: Yes — section 211 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 contains a proviso that extends this benefit even to such presumptive-tax assessees. While clause (b) of section 211(1) requires an assessee declaring profits under section 44AD(1) or section 44ADA(1) to pay the whole advance tax on or before 15th March[1], the proviso to section 211(1) states that any amount paid by way of advance tax on or before the 31st day of March shall also be treated as advance tax paid during the financial year ending on that day for all purposes of the Act[1]. This proviso is not restricted to the four-instalment assessees under clause (a); it applies generally, so an assessee under section 44AD(1) or 44ADA(1) who pays advance tax any time up to 31st March, even after the 15th March due date, will still have that payment treated as advance tax paid within that financial year[1].

(2) Theft is robbery if, in order to the committing of the theft, or in committing the theft, or in carrying away or attempting to carry away property obtained by the theft, the offender, for that end voluntarily causes or attempts to cause to any person death or hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death or of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint. (3) Extortion is robbery if the offender, at the time of committing the extortion, is in the presence of the person put in fear, and commits the extortion by putting that person in fear of instant death, of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint to that person or to some other person, and, by so putting in fear, induces the person so put in fear then and there to deliver up the thing extorted. Explanation.—The offender is said to be present if he is sufficiently near to put the other person in fear of instant death, of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint. Illustrations. (a) A holds Z down, and fraudulently takes Z’s money and jewels from Z’s clothes, without Z’s consent. Here A has committed theft, and, in order to the committing of that theft, has voluntarily caused wrongful restraint to Z. A has therefore committed robbery. (b) A meets Z on the high road, shows a pistol, and demands Z’s purse. Z, in consequence, surrenders his purse. Here A has extorted the purse from Z by putting him in fear of instant hurt, and being at the time of committing the extortion in his presence. A has therefore committed robbery. (c) A meets Z and Z’s child on the high road. A takes the child, and threatens to fling it down a precipice, unless Z delivers his purse. Z, in consequence, delivers his purse. Here A has extorted the purse from Z, by causing Z to be in fear of instant hurt to the child who is there present. A has therefore committed robbery on Z. (d) A obtains property from Z by saying—"Your child is in the hands of my gang, and will be put to death unless you send us ten thousand rupees". This is extortion, and punishable as such; but it is not robbery, unless Z is put in fear of the instant death of his child. retrieved_context.text: (1) In all robbery there is either theft or extortion. (2) Theft is robbery if, in order to the committing of the theft, or in committing the theft, or in carrying away or attempting to carry away property obtained by the theft, the offender, for that end voluntarily causes or attempts to cause to any person death or hurt or wrongful restraint, or fear of instant death or of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint. (3) Extortion is robbery if the offender, at the time of committing the extortion, is in the presence of the person put in fear, and commits the extortion by putting that person in fear of instant death, of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint to that person or to some other person, and, by so putting in fear, induces the person so put in fear then and there to deliver up the thing extorted. Explanation.—The offender is said to be present if he is sufficiently near to put the other person in fear of instant death, of instant hurt, or of instant wrongful restraint. Illustrations. (a) A holds Z down, and fraudulently takes Z’s money and jewels from Z’s clothes, without Z’s consent. Here A has committed theft, and, in order to the committing of that theft, has voluntarily caused wrongful restraint to Z. A has therefore committed robbery. (b) A meets Z on the high road, shows a pistol, and demands Z’s purse. Z, in consequence, surrenders his purse. Here A has extorted the purse from Z by putting him in fear of instant hurt, and being at the time of committing the extortion in his presence. A has therefore committed robbery. (c) A meets Z and Z’s child on the high road. A takes the child, and threatens to fling it down a precipice, unless Z delivers his purse. Z, in consequence, delivers his purse. Here A has extorted the purse from Z, by causing Z to be in fear of instant hurt to the child who is there present. A has therefore committed robbery on Z. (d) A obtains property from Z by saying—"Your child is in the hands of my gang, and will be put to death unless you send us ten thousand rupees". This is extortion, and punishable as such; but it is not robbery, unless Z is put in fear of the instant death of his child. (4) Whoever commits robbery shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine; and, if the robbery be committed on the highway between sunset and sunrise, the imprisonment may be extended to fourteen years. (5) Whoever attempts to commit robbery shall be punished with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years, and shall also be liable to fine. (6) If any person, in committing or in attempting to commit robbery, voluntarily causes hurt, such person, and any other person jointly concerned in committing or attempting to commit such robbery, shall be punished with imprisonment for life, or with rigorous imprisonment for a term which may extend to ten years, and shall also be liable to fine.

reference.answer: When the Central Government and the patentee cannot agree on compensation for a patent acquired under Section 102 for a public purpose, the dispute as to the amount of compensation payable is to be referred to the High Court under Section 103, by either party, in the manner prescribed by the rules of the High Court[2]. In default of agreement, the High Court determines the compensation as it thinks just, having regard to (i) the expenditure incurred in connection with the invention, (ii) in the case of a patent, its term, (iii) the period during which and the manner in which it has already been worked, including the profits made during such period by the patentee or by his licensee (whether exclusive or otherwise), and (iv) other relevant factors[1].

Opening a new metro station is a "work" covered by Section 16, which expressly applies the Section 14/15 procedure (including the Commissioner's prior inspection and report requirements) to the "opening of stations and junctions" constructed after the Commissioner's Section 15 report[1]. By contrast, Section 17 allows the original tracks and works restored after an accident, or a temporary diversion laid to restore communication, to be opened for public carriage of passengers "without prior inspection by the Commissioner," subject only to a written certification by the official in charge and immediate notice to the Commissioner[2]. Thus the opening of a new station remains subject to prior Commissioner inspection under Sections 14 and 15 as extended by Section 16[1], whereas the temporary diversion after an accident can be opened without such prior inspection, on satisfying the certification and notice conditions in Section 17[2].

Because the descriptive word is "common to the trade or is otherwise of a non-distinctive character," registration of the composite label does not confer any exclusive right in that word standing alone as "matter forming only a part of the whole"[1]. reference.answer: Yes, the two provisions are textually identical in both their grounds for removal and their restoration procedure. Under both Section 20 of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949 and Section 20 of the Cost Accountants Act, 1959, the Council may remove a member's name from the Register on the same four grounds: death, request by the member, non-payment of prescribed fee, or subjection to disabilities under Section 8 or other reasons for ceasing entitlement[1][2]. Both provisions also mandate removal where an order under the Act has been passed removing the person from membership. For restoration, both Acts contain an identical sub-section (3) mechanism: where removal was under clause (c) (non-payment of fee), the member may, on application, have his name entered again in the Register upon payment of arrears of annual fee and entrance fee along with such additional fee as the Council may determine by notification[1][2].

Question: Comparing Section 11DDA of the Central Excise Act, 1944 with Section 28BA of the Customs Act, 1962, both dealing with provisional attachment of property to protect revenue: are the maximum duration of attachment, the approving authority, and the exclusion of settlement commission proceedings from the limitation period structured in the same way under both provisions?

reference.answer:
Yes, the two provisions are structured in an identical manner on all three points.

### Maximum duration
Under both Section 11DDA of the Central Excise Act, 1944 and Section 28BA of the Customs Act, 1962, provisional attachment ceases to have effect after six months from the date of the order, extendable for reasons recorded in writing, but the total period of extension cannot exceed two years in either statute[1][2].

### Approving authority
The order of provisional attachment must be made with the previous approval of the Principal Commissioner/Commissioner (of Central Excise under Section 11DDA, of Customs under Section 28BA), and any extension is granted by the Principal Chief Commissioner/Chief Commissioner in identical terms under both sections[1][2].

### Exclusion for settlement proceedings
Both provisions contain an identical exclusion mechanism: where an application for settlement of the case is made to the Settlement Commission, the period from the date of that application until the date of the order under the corresponding settlement-order provision is excluded from the limitation period for extension — Section 32-E/32-F under the Central Excise Act[1] and Section 127B/127C under the Customs Act[2].

reference.answer: A party is barred from leading such evidence whenever the language of the document is plain in itself and that plain language applies accurately to the existing facts[1]. In that situation, extrinsic evidence cannot be admitted to show the document was intended to apply to different facts, as illustrated by the sale of "my estate at Rampur containing 100 bighas," where evidence that a differently situated or sized estate was actually meant cannot be given once the description accurately fits an existing estate of that description[1]. reference.answer: These two provisions differ fundamentally in how the limitation period and form of appeal are fixed: Section 202 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 does not itself prescribe any specific limitation period or form, instead leaving the form, period, and manner of appeal to the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal to be "specified by regulations"[1]. In contrast, Section 61A of the Insurance Act, 1938 directly fixes the limitation period in the statute itself, requiring that an appeal "be filed within a period of forty-five days" from receipt of the Tribunal's order, in a prescribed form and accompanied by a prescribed fee[2], with a proviso allowing condonation of delay beyond forty-five days on sufficient cause[2]. Thus, Section 202 delegates the fixing of the appeal period and form to subordinate regulations, whereas Section 61A itself lays down a fixed statutory period of forty-five days with a built-in condonation clause[1][2].

reference.answer: Under Section 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the power arises during the pendency of a suit before the Court, at the point where "it appears to the Court that there exist elements of a settlement which may be acceptable to the parties"[1]. reference.answer: Section 203 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 confers jurisdiction on any Court through or into whose local limits the person (by or against whom the offence is committed) or the thing (in respect of which it is committed) "passed" while on a journey or voyage, meaning that mere transit of that person or thing through the Court's territory during the journey is sufficient to found jurisdiction[1]. The provision's language — "may be inquired into or tried by a Court through or into whose local jurisdiction that person or thing passed in the course of that journey or voyage" — does not require that the offence itself have occurred within that Court's territorial limits; it is enough that the journey passed through the area, so the section extends jurisdiction beyond the place where the offending act or its consequence actually took place[1]. The excerpts do not elaborate further on how this "passing through" test is applied in practice or how it interacts with other jurisdiction provisions.

reference.answer: Yes. Under Section 261(2) of the Cantonments Act, 2006, the Chief Executive Officer may direct removal of a boundary wall considered "unsuitable, unsightly or otherwise objectionable," but the proviso separately entitles the owner to compensation from the Board whenever the wall was erected with the CEO's consent/orders or was in existence at the commencement of the Act, regardless of whether it was found unsuitable or objectionable[1]. The compensation entitlement is tied to the wall's origin/timing (pre-existing at commencement or CEO-sanctioned construction), not to any finding that it was suitable or unobjectionable[1].

reference.answer: Section 54L comes into play at the stage where the Adjudicating Authority has to decide on a resolution plan already approved by the committee of creditors under section 54K (sub-section (4) or (12)), and it requires the Authority to approve such a plan, within thirty days of receipt, if it meets the requirements of sub-section (2) of section 30 and has provisions for effective implementation[1]. It thus governs the pre-packaged insolvency resolution process rather than the ordinary corporate insolvency resolution process, as shown by its cross-reference to committee decisions "of section 54K" and to an order passed "under sub-section (2) of section 54J"[1]. If the plan does not meet the requirements, or if it does not result in a change of management/control of the corporate debtor to a non-promoter as contemplated under section 54J(2), the Authority must reject the plan and, in the latter case, terminate the pre-packaged process and pass a liquidation order under section 33(1)(b)[1]. Contravention of a resolution plan approved under section 54L(1) is treated, for the purpose of seeking a liquidation order, on the same footing as contravention of a plan approved under section 31[1][2]. Liquidation orders passed under section 54L(4) are separately appealable on grounds of material irregularity or fraud[3].

Question: Under Section 200 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, what does it mean to say that ratification of an unauthorized act 'cannot injure a third person' - i.e., in what sense is a principal barred from ratifying an act that would subject a third party to damages or terminate their rights?

Dataset answer requirements:
- Answer the question directly in the first sentence.

reference.answer:
Section 200 means that although ratification ordinarily relates back and gives the unauthorized act the same effect as if it had been authorized from the start[1], this retroactive effect is specifically denied where the unauthorized act, had it been authorized, would have subjected a third person to damages or terminated that third person's existing right or interest[1]. In other words, a principal cannot use ratification as a device to retrospectively create a liability in, or extinguish a right of, a third party who was not privy to the unauthorized dealing and had no opportunity to resist it at the time it was done[1].

The illustrations make the scope concrete: where an unauthorized person demands delivery of a chattel on the principal's behalf, the principal's later ratification cannot make the person in possession liable in damages for having refused to deliver, because that liability would arise only from the (absent) authority, not from the principal's after-the-fact approval[1]. Likewise, where an unauthorized person serves a notice terminating a lease, the principal's ratification cannot bind the tenant to that termination, since it would extinguish the tenant's subsisting right to remain until proper notice is given[1]. This operates as a specific limitation on the general rule that ratification "ratifies the whole of the transaction" and produces the same effects as prior authority[1] - that general effect is cut down whenever the third person would otherwise be worse off by damages or loss of rights solely because of the ratification.

reference.answer:
Section 227 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to Section 204 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, both titled "Issue of process" and containing identically worded sub-sections (1) to (4) on issuing summons/warrants after taking cognizance, requiring a list of prosecution witnesses before issuance, accompanying complaints with process, and dismissal for non-payment of process-fees[1].

The substantive change introduced in Section 227 is the addition of a proviso to sub-section (1) stating that "summons or warrants may also be issued through electronic means"[1], a provision absent from the corresponding text of Section 204 of the old Code, which only speaks of issuing a warrant or summons for the accused to be brought or to appear before the Magistrate without reference to electronic issuance[1]. Apart from this addition permitting electronic-mode issuance, the core requirements—such as the mandatory filing of a witness list before issuance of process[1]—remain the same in both provisions.

Which provision of the new Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 corresponds to this section, and does its substantive content differ from the old provision?

reference.answer:
Section 392 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 corresponds to Section 433 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023[1].

The text of the two provisions is identical: both provide that where an appeal under the relevant Chapter is heard by a High Court Bench of Judges and the Judges are divided in opinion, the appeal along with their opinions shall be laid before another Judge of that Court, who shall deliver his opinion after such hearing as he thinks fit, and the judgment or order shall follow that opinion, subject to the proviso that if one of the Judges of the original Bench, or the Judge before whom the appeal is so laid, requires it, the appeal shall instead be re-heard and decided by a larger Bench of Judges[1]. On the basis of the excerpts, there is no substantive difference between the old Section 392 and the new Section 433; the wording is verbatim the same[1].

reference.answer:
No — a bare, unsubstantiated oral assertion of prior payment, without anything probable brought on record, is not sufficient to rebut the presumption under Section 139[2].

The excerpt on rebuttal standards holds that while an accused need not prove his defence beyond reasonable doubt, "bare denial of the passing of the consideration and existence of debt... would not serve[] the purpose of the accused" and "something which is probable has to be brought on record" to shift the burden back to the complainant[1]. This indicates that a mere oral claim of payment, unaccompanied by any probable or corroborating material, would fall short of what is required to rebut the statutory presumption that the cheque was received for discharge of a debt or liability[2][1].

reference.answer:
Yes, the excerpts establish that the ingredients of Section 138 — presentation of the cheque within its validity period, dishonour due to insufficiency of funds, issuance of a demand notice within thirty days of receiving information of dishonour, and failure of the drawer to pay within fifteen days of receipt of that notice — are cumulative, and all of them must be proved before the offence is made out.

### Analysis
The statutory text itself frames clauses (a), (b) and (c) as a proviso stating that "nothing contained in this section shall apply unless" each of these conditions is satisfied[2], indicating that all three conditions are conjunctive prerequisites to the offence.

A Delhi District Court decision expressly listed five ingredients — valid presentation, a legally enforceable debt, dishonour for insufficiency of funds, a written demand notice within thirty days, and failure to pay within fifteen days of notice — and held that "the accused can only be held guilty of the offence under Section 138 NI Act if all of the above-mentioned ingredients are proved by the complainant co-extensively"[1], in addition to the conditions under Section 142 of the Act.

Other decisions similarly emphasize that "the ingredients thereof are required to be proved" for the offence to be made out[2], and that clauses (b) and (c) of the proviso "must be read together"[2], reinforcing that these are interlinked, cumulative requirements rather than independent or alternative conditions.

reference.answer:
The excerpts do not give a single settled answer — they show a split in the Delhi District Court decisions on this point.

### Position favouring presumption of service
Several decisions hold that even where the notice is sent only under Certificate of Posting (UPC), if it is dispatched with the correct address of the drawer written on it, a presumption of service arises[1]. This reasoning imports the principle underlying Section 27 of the General Clauses Act into Section 138 proceedings, so that service is deemed effected unless the drawer proves that it was not in fact received and that he was not responsible for the non-service; a bald denial by the accused, without examining a witness from the postal department, is not enough to displace this presumption[2].

### Contrary position requiring proof of service
Another decision, relying on a Gujarat High Court ruling, holds that in the case of a notice sent only under certificate of posting, it cannot be deemed to have been served[3]. In that case, where the accused specifically denied receipt and there were discrepancies between the date of the notice and the date of the UPC, the court held it was necessary for the complainant to affirmatively prove due service by examining a postal official to properly prove the UPC, rather than relying on any presumption[3].

### What this means
Because the excerpts contain both lines of reasoning without indicating which is authoritative, the provided local sources do not offer a single definitive rule; the outcome in the excerpts appears to turn on facts such as whether the address was correct, whether there were discrepancies in dates, and whether the accused's denial was specific and unrebutted[1][2][3].

reference.answer:
Courts in the excerpts have treated the Section 146 presumption of dishonour as standing unrebutted where the accused merely denies the fact without leading any evidence or disputing the correctness of the dishonour memo, holding the "defence has failed to rebut the said presumption"[1].

### Applicable law
Section 146 makes production of a bank's dishonour memo bearing the official mark prima facie proof of dishonour, presumed unless disproved[2]. Section 139 similarly presumes, unless the contrary is proved, that the cheque was received for discharge of a debt or liability[3].

### Relevant judgments
In one case, the accused denied receipt of the legal notice but "has not led any evidence to establish the same," and the court held the presumption of dishonour under the bank memo stood because the "defence has failed to rebut the said presumption"[1]. Where the excerpts show that the cheque was proved to have been given merely as collateral security and not in discharge of a legally enforceable debt existing at the time of issuance, courts have held that no offence under Section 138 is made out at all, so a complaint founded on such a cheque fails and any conviction/summoning based on it cannot stand.

### Reasoning in the excerpts
Section 138 itself defines "debt or other liability" as a legally enforceable debt or other liability, making this a statutory ingredient of the offence [1 - via s.138]. Courts applying this have held that dishonour of a cheque given as security does not make out an offence under Section 138, especially where payment was tied to a future date and no debt or liability existed on the date the cheque was delivered[1]. Consequently, where a cheque is issued not for discharge of any debt or liability, its dishonour does not attract penal consequences and the drawer "shall not... be liable for prosecution"[2]. Another court similarly held that proceedings under Section 138 "cannot be initiated when a cheque is given as security," distinguishing liability from security, since Section 138 applies only when a cheque is issued to clear a liability[2][3]. A further judgment reiterates that the cheque must be issued in discharge of a debt or liability that is "subsisting and legally enforceable at the time of its issuance," and that a cheque issued towards a non-existent liability (such as security) falls outside Section 138's purview[4].

The excerpts establish that once it is proved the cheque was security rather than discharge of a debt, no presumption under Section 138 arises and no offence is made out, defeating the complaint on merits[1][2][3][4]; they do not, however, separately discuss the procedural mechanics of quashing a summoning order under Section 142, so that specific point is not addressed by these sources.

retrieved_context.text: Any guarantee which the creditor has obtained by means of keeping silence as to material circumstances, is invalid. (b) A guarantees to C payment for iron to be supplied by him to B to the amount of 2,000 tons. A is not liable as a surety.
